'''tranation†''' (trạ̄-nā′shon), ''n.'' [< L. ''tranare'' (''transnare''), pp. ''tranatus'', swim across, < ''trans'', across, + ''nare'', swim: see ''natant''.] The act of passing over by swimming; transnatation.

'''trance<sup>1</sup>''' (trȧns), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''transe'', ''traunce'', < OF. *''transe'', passage (found only in the deflected sense: see ''trance''<sup>2</sup>), = It. ''transito'', passage, < L. ''transitus'', a crossing over, transit: see ''transit''. Cf. ''trance''<sup>2</sup>.] 1. A journeying or
readings.c3s1:
journey over a country; especially, a tedious journey. [Old and prov. Eng.]—2. A passage, especially a passage inside a house. [Scotch.]

{{smaller block|But mair he look'd, and dule saw he,
On the door at the ''trance'',
Spots o' his dear ladys bluid
Shining like a lance.
{{right|''Lammikin'' (Child's Ballads, III. 311).}}}}

'''trance<sup>1</sup>†''' (trȧns), ''v. i.'' [Early mod. E. also ''traunce''; < ''trance''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] To tramp; travel.

{{smaller block|''Traunce'' the world over, you shall never purse up so much gold as when you were in England.
{{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', Fair Maid of the Inn, v. 2.}}}}

'''trance<sup>2</sup>''' (trȧns), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''transe'', ''traunce''; < ME. ''trance'', ''transe'', ''traunce'', < OF. ''transe'', extreme fear, dread, a trance or swoon (prob. also in orig. sense 'passage'), F. ''transe'', extreme fear, = Sp. ''trance'', critical moment, crisis, hour of death, transfer of goods, = Pg. ''trance'', critical moment, crisis, hour of death, = It. ''transito'', passage, decease, < L. ''transitus'', a passage, < ''transire'', pass over: see ''transit'', and cf. ''trance''<sup>1</sup>. Some derive F. ''transe'' directly from OF. ''transi'', fallen in a swoon, amazed, half-dead, pp. of ''transir'', fall in a swoon, lit. go over.] 1. A passing away or apart; a state in which the soul seems to have passed out of the body into another state of being; a state of insensibility to mundane things; a rapture; an ecstasy.

{{smaller block|Now hast thou sit as in a ''trance'', and seen
To thy soul's joy, and honour of thy house,
The trophies and the triumphs of thy men.
{{right|''Peele'', Battle of Alcazar, v.}}}}
readings.c3s2:
¶
{{smaller block|While they made ready, he fell into a ''trance'', and saw heaven opened.
{{right|Acts x. 10, 11.}}}}

{{smaller block|Some haue their supernaturall ''traunces'' or rauishments: some dwell amongst men, some by themselues apart.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 307.}}}}

2. A state of perplexity or bewilderment; amaze.

{{smaller block|Both stood like old acquaintance in a ''trance'',
Met far from home, wondering each other's chance.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 1595.}}}}

3. In ''med.'', catalepsy; ecstasy; the hypnotic state.

'''trance'''<sup>2</sup> (trȧns), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''tranced'', ppr. ''trancing''. [< ''trance''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'' Cf. ''entrance''<sup>2</sup>.] 1. To entrance; place in or as in a trance or rapture.

{{smaller block|The trumpets sounded,
And there I left him ''tranced''.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, v. 3. 218.}}}}

{{smaller block|I trod as one ''tranced'' in some rapturous vision.
{{right|''Shelley'', Revolt of Islam, v. 17.}}}}

2. To hold or bind with or as with a charm or spell; overspread or shroud as with a spell; charm; enchant.

{{smaller block|A ''tranced'' summer-night.
{{right|''Keats'', Hyperion, i.}}}}

'''trancedly''' (trȧn′sed-li), ''adv.'' In a trance-like or spell-bound manner; like one in a trance.

{{smaller block|Then stole I up, and ''trancedly''
Gazed on the Persian girl alone.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Arabian Nights.}}}}

'''tranché''' (F. pron. troṅ-shā′), ''a.'' [F., pp. of ''trancher'', cut: see ''trench''.] In ''her.'', party per bend.

'''tranect†''', ''n.'' See the quotation under ''traject.''

'''traneen''' (trā-nēn′), ''n.'' [< Ir. ''trainīn, traithnīn,'' a little stalk of grass, the herb-bennet.] A grass, ''Cynosurus cristatus. Britten and Holland.'' [Irish.]—'''Not worth a traneen,''' {{smaller|not worth a rush.}}

'''trangam†, trangame†''', ''n.'' Same as ''trangram.''

'''trangle''' (trang′gl), ''n.'' [Origin obscure.] In ''her.,'' one of the diminutives of the fesse, by some writers considered as a bar, by others as a closet or barrulet.

'''trangram†''' (trang′gram), ''n.'' [Also ''trangam, trangame, trankum;'' appar. an arbitrary var. of ''tangram'' or perhaps of ''anagram.''] Something trumpery, unusual, or of no value; a gimcrack.

{{smaller block|But go, thou ''Trangame,'' and carry back those ''Trangames,'' which thou hast stol'n or purloin'd.
{{right|''Wycherley,'' Plain Dealer, iii. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|What a devil 's the meaning of all these ''trangrams'' and gimcracks, gentlemen? ''Arbuthnot,'' Hist. John Bull, iii. 6.}}

{{smaller block|"But, hey-day, what, have you taken the chain and medal off from my bonnet?" "And meet time it was, when yon usher, vinegar-faced rogue that he is, began to inquire what popish ''trangam'' you were wearing."
{{right|''Scott,'' Abbot, xix.}}}}

'''trank''' (trangk), ''n.'' [Origin obscure.] In ''glove-making,'' an oblong piece taken from the skin, from which the shape of the glove is cut by a knife in a press. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''tranka''' (trang′kä), ''n.'' A long cylindrical box balanced and juggled with by the feet of an acrobat.

{{RunningHeader|tramp|6425|trapdoor}}Sw. Norw. ''trampa'' = Dan. ''trampe'', tramp, stamp, tread, trample, a secondary verb, from a strong verb seen in Goth. ''anatrimpan'', tread upon (press upon); perhaps ult. akin to ''trap'', D. G. ''trappen'', tread: see ''trap''1, ''trap''2.] I. ''trans.'' 1. To tread under foot; trample. {{smaller block|It is like unto the camamele; the more ye tread it and ''trampe'' it, the sweter it smelleth, the thicker it groweth, the better it spreddeth. {{right|''T. Stapleton'', Fortress of the Faith (1565). (''Latham.'')}}}} 2. To tread (clothes) in water, so as to cleanse or scour them. [Scotch.]—3. To travel over on foot: as, to ''tramp'' a country. II. ''intrans.'' 1. To walk, especially to walk with heavy step; tread; march; go on foot. {{smaller block|How often did he . . . dread to look over his shoulder, lest he should behold some uncouth being ''tramping'' close behind him! {{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 425.}}}} {{smaller block|He had ''tramped'' about the fields of the vacant farm, trying helplessly to look after things which he did not understand. {{right|''Mrs. Oliphant'', Poor Gentleman, v.}}}} 2. To go about as a vagrant or vagabond. '''tramp''' (tramp), ''n.'' [< ''tramp'', ''v.''] 1. The sound made by the feet in walking or marching. {{smaller block|Then came the ''tramp'' of horse. {{right|''Scott'', Antiquary, xxvi.}}}} {{smaller block|The unmercifully lengthened ''tramp'' of my passing and returning footsteps. {{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 38.}}}} 2. An excursion or journey on foot; a walk. {{smaller block|It was his delight . . . to organize woodland ''tramps'', and to start us on researches similar to his own. {{right|''H. B. Stowe'', Oldtown, p. 429.}}}} {{smaller block|We shook hands with them all, men, women, and children, resuming our ''tramp'' about eleven o'clock. We still kept the main traveled road. {{right|''The Century'', XL. 615.}}}} '''3.''' A plate of iron worn by ditchers, etc., under the hollow of the foot, to save the shoe in pressing the spade into the earth.—'''4.''' An instrument for trimming hedges.—'''5.''' An itinerant mechanic: same as ''tramper'', 2.—'''6.''' An idle vagrant; a homeless vagabond. Also ''tramper''. {{smaller block|Another class, that of importunate sturdy ''tramps'', has been perambulating the country, composed generally of young, idle, and insolent able-bodied men, unamenable to discipline, threatening and committing lawless acts of violence in the workhouses where they obtain nightly shelter. {{right|''A. Owen'', quoted in Ribton-Turner's Vagrants and [Vagrancy, p. 267.}}}} {{smaller block|The “sturdy beggars” who infested England two or three centuries ago reappear in our midst under the name of ''tramps.'' {{right|''J. F. Clarke'', Self-Culture, p. 280.}}}} 7. A freight-vessel that does not run in any regular line, but takes a cargo wherever the shippers desire: also used attributively, as in ''tramp steamer.'' Also called ''ocean tramp.'' [Slang.] '''tramper''' (tram′pėr), ''n.'' [< ''tramp'' + ''-er''1.] 1. One who tramps.—2. An itinerant mechanic; a workman in search of employment.—3. An idle vagrant; a homeless vagabond; a tramp; a gipsy. {{smaller block|They had suddenly perceived . . . a party of gipsies. . . . How the ''trampers'' might have behaved had the young ladies been more courageous must be doubtful; but such an invitation for attack could not be resisted. {{right|''Jane Austen'', Emma, xxxix.}}}} {{smaller block|D'ye think his honour has naething else to do than to speak wi' ilka idle ''tramper'' that comes about the town? {{right|''Scott'', Heart of Mid-Lothian, xxvi.}}}} '''tramping-drum''' (tram′ping-drum), ''n.'' In the manufacture of leather, a stuffing-wheel with hollow trunnions, through which warm air or steam is circulated into and out of the drum, while saturating in it a quantity of leather with oil. '''tram-plate''' (tram′plāt), ''n.'' A flat iron plate laid as a rail: the earliest form of rail for railways. '''trample''' (tram′pl), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''trampled'', ppr. ''trampling''. [< ME. ''trampelen'', ''tramplen'' = D. ''trampelen'' = LG. ''trampeln'' = MHG. ''trampeln'', G. ''trampeln''; a freq. of ''tramp''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To beat or tread down by the tramping or stamping of feet, or by frequent treading; prostrate or crush by treading under foot; tread upon or tread down, literally or figuratively. {{smaller block|Neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they ''trample'' them under their feet. {{right|Mat. vii. 6.}}}} {{smaller block|But that Humane and Diuine learning is now ''trampled'' vnder the barbarous foote of the Ottoman-Horse. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 320.}}}} {{smaller block|Was it not enough for thee to stoop so low for our sakes, but that thou shouldst be ''trampled'' on because thou didst it? {{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, I. vi.}}}} {{smaller block|Squadrons of the Prince, ''trampling'' the flowers. {{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, v.}}}} {{smaller block|In 1869 the present ruler of Austria and Dalmatia strove . . . to ''trample'' under foot the ancient rights of the freemen of the Bocche di Cattaro. {{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Venice, p. 236.}}}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' To tread with repeated force and shock; stamp; hence, to tramp roughshod; tread roughly or contemptuously. {{smaller block|My Muse, to some eares not vnsweet, Tempers her words to ''trampling'' horses' feete More oft then to a chamber-melodie. {{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Astrophel and Stella, lxxxiv.}}}} {{smaller block|Certaine others . . . gathered their ananas in the Indians gardens, ''trampling'' through them without any discretion. {{right|''Hakluyt's Voyages'', III. 320.}}}} {{smaller block|'Tis the presumptuous and proud man alone who dares to ''trample'' on those truths which the rest of the world reverence. {{right|''Bp. Atterbury'', Sermons, I. v.}}}} {{smaller block|I ''trample'' on your offers and on you. {{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, iv.}}}} {{smaller block|Sudden and steady the music, as eight hoofs ''trample'' and thunder. {{right|''Swinburne'', Hesperia.}}}} '''trample''' (tram′pl), ''n.'' [< ''trample'', ''v.''] A frequent heavy or rough tread; a trampling. {{smaller block|Under the despiteful control, the ''trample'' and spurn of all the other damned. {{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., ii.}}}} {{smaller block|The sound is drawing close, And speedier than the ''trample'' of speedy feet it goes. {{right|''W. Morris'', Sigurd, ii.}}}} '''trampler''' (tram′plėr), ''n.'' [< ''trample'' + ''-er''1.] 1. One who tramples.—2†. A lawyer. {{smaller block|Pity your ''trampler'', sir, your poor solicitor. {{right|''Middleton'', World Tost at Tennis.}}}} {{smaller block|The ''trampler'' is in hast, O cleere the way, Takes fees with both hands cause he cannot stay, No matter wheth'r the cause be right or wrong, So hee be payd for letting out his tongue. {{right|''John Taylor'', Works (1630). (''Nares.'')}}}} '''trampoose''', ''v. i.'' See ''trampous.'' '''trampot''' (tram′pot), ''n.'' [< ''tram''1 + ''pot.''] In ''milling'', the support in which the foot of the spindle is stepped. [[File:century v08 p0229 c2f1.png|center|321px]] {{c|Trampots.}} {{c|1. Arched trampot, the arch at ''c'' straddling a driving-shaft when bevel-gearing is used; ''a'', bridge-tree supporting the step ''b''. 2. More common form of trampot, in which the movable step is adjustable to center by a quadrilateral arrangement of set-screws.}} '''trampous, trampoose''' (tram′pus, tram-pös′), ''v. i.''; pret. and pp. ''trampoused'', ''trampoosed'', ppr. ''trampousing'', ''trampoosing''. [Appar. < ''tramp'' + ''-ous'', ''-oose'', a merely capricious addition.] To tramp; walk or wander about. [Vulgar.] {{smaller block|Some years ago I landed near to Dover,
And seed strange sights, ''trampoosing'' England over. {{right|''D. Humphreys'', The Yankee in England. (''Bartlett.'')}}}} '''tramp-pick''' (tramp′pik), ''n.'' A kind of lever of iron, about 4 feet long and 1 inch in breadth and thickness, tapering away at the lower end and having a small degree of curvature there, somewhat like the prong of a dung-fork, used for turning up very hard soils. {{smaller|It is fitted with a rest, about 18 inches from the lower end, on which the workman presses with his foot.}} '''tramroad''' (tram′rōd), ''n.'' [Formerly also (once) ''dramroad'' (a form appar. due to the D. cognate); < ''tram''1, a rail, + ''road''.] A road in which the track for the wheels is made of pieces of wood, flat stones, or plates of iron laid in line; a tramway. See ''tramway''. '''tram-staff''' (tram′stȧf), ''n.'' In ''milling'', a straightedge used to test the position of the spindle and millstone, and to test the surface of the stone. {{smaller|One form is called the ''red-staff'', because it is rubbed with red chalk or other coloring matter, and leaves a red mark on all prominent points it encounters in passing over the surface of the stone.}} '''tramway''' (tram′wā), ''n.'' [< ''tram''1, a rail, + ''way''1.] The earliest form of railroad. {{smaller|It consisted at first of trams of wood or flat stones, at a later period of wooden stringers covered with strap-iron, and lastly of iron rails. The first tramways were simply rude horse-railroads for the transportation of heavy freight. The term is now applied to all kinds of street-railroads, whether using engines, horses, a cable, or electricity. [Great Britain.]}} {{smaller block|The smelting furnaces are the centre of activity, and to them ''tramways'' and railways converge, bearing strings of trucks loaded with materials. {{right|''Edinburgh Rev.'', CXVII. 211.}}}} '''tram-wheel''' (tram′hwēl), ''n.'' The form of light, flanged, metallic wheel usual on tram-cars. [[File:century v08 p0229 c2f2.png|center|135px]] {{c|Train-wheel.}} ¶ '''tranation†''' (trạ̄-nā′shon), ''n.'' [< L.
